items.title: Exercise 1. Bernoulli rate–distortion
items.prompt:
Let $X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)$, $p\le1/2$, with

$$
d(x,\widehat x)=\mathbf1\{x\ne\widehat x\}.
$$


1. Prove the lower bound
   $$
   I(X;\widehat X)\ge h_2(p)-h_2(D)
   $$
   for $0\le D\le p$.

2. Construct a test channel that attains equality.

3. Explain why $R(D)=0$ for $D\ge p$.
items.answer:
Let

$$
P_e=P(X\ne\widehat X)\le D.
$$

Because $X$ is binary, $\widehat X$ together with the error indicator $E=\mathbf1\{X\ne\widehat X\}$ determines $X$. Hence

$$
H(X\mid\widehat X)
\le H(E\mid\widehat X)
\le H(E)
=h_2(P_e).
$$

For $0\le D\le p\le1/2$, $h_2$ is increasing, so

$$
H(X\mid\widehat X)
\le h_2(P_e)
\le h_2(D).
$$

Therefore

$$
\boxed{
I(X;\widehat X)
=H(X)-H(X\mid\widehat X)
\ge h_2(p)-h_2(D)
}.
$$

To attain equality, it is convenient to specify the **backward** test channel. Let

$$
\widehat X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q),
\qquad
Z\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(D)
$$

be independent, and define

$$
X=\widehat X\oplus Z.
$$

Then $P(X\ne\widehat X)=D$, while

$$
P(X=1)=D+q(1-2D).
$$

Choose

$$
q=\frac{p-D}{1-2D},
$$

which is valid for $0\le D\le p\le1/2$ (with the boundary case $p=D=1/2$ handled separately). The marginal of $X$ is then $\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)$, and

$$
H(X\mid\widehat X)=H(Z)=h_2(D).
$$

Thus

$$
I(X;\widehat X)=h_2(p)-h_2(D).
$$

The forward channel $P(\widehat x\mid x)$ follows from Bayes' rule applied to this joint distribution.

For $D\ge p$, the decoder can always emit $\widehat X=0$. The rate is then zero and the average distortion is $P(X=1)=p\le D$. Therefore

$$
R(D)=0,
\qquad D\ge p.
$$

---

items.title: Exercise 2. Predictive IB distortion
items.prompt:
For the Markov chain $Y\to X\to T$, prove

$$
I(X;Y)-I(T;Y)
=
\mathbb E_{X,T}
D_{\mathrm{KL}}
\bigl(P_{Y\mid X}\|P_{Y\mid T}\bigr).
$$

Show that minimizing $I(X;T)-\beta I(T;Y)$ is equivalent to a rate–distortion Lagrangian with this distortion.
items.answer:
The chain rule gives

$$
I(X,T;Y)=I(T;Y)+I(X;Y\mid T)
$$

and also

$$
I(X,T;Y)=I(X;Y)+I(T;Y\mid X).
$$

For the Markov chain $Y\to X\to T$,

$$
I(T;Y\mid X)=0.
$$

Therefore

$$
I(X;Y)-I(T;Y)=I(X;Y\mid T).
$$

Conditional mutual information is an average KL divergence:

$$
I(X;Y\mid T)
=
\mathbb E_{X,T}
D_{\mathrm{KL}}
\bigl(P_{Y\mid X,T}\|P_{Y\mid T}\bigr).
$$

Markovity gives $P_{Y\mid X,T}=P_{Y\mid X}$, hence

$$
\boxed{
I(X;Y)-I(T;Y)
=
\mathbb E_{X,T}
D_{\mathrm{KL}}
\bigl(P_{Y\mid X}\|P_{Y\mid T}\bigr)
}.
$$

Calling the KL term $d_{\mathrm{IB}}(X,T)$,

$$
I(X;T)-\beta I(T;Y)
=
I(X;T)+\beta\mathbb E[d_{\mathrm{IB}}(X,T)]-\beta I(X;Y).
$$

The last term does not depend on $P_{T\mid X}$. The minimizers therefore coincide with those of the rate–distortion Lagrangian

$$
I(X;T)+\beta\mathbb E[d_{\mathrm{IB}}(X,T)].
$$

---

items.title: Exercise 3. Variational VIB bounds
items.prompt:
1. Prove
   $$
   I(T;Y)
   \ge
   H(Y)+\mathbb E[\log r_\psi(Y\mid T)].
   $$

2. Prove
   $$
   \mathbb E_XD_{\mathrm{KL}}(q(T\mid X)\|r(T))
   =
   I(X;T)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q(T)\|r(T)).
   $$

3. Explain when both bounds are tight simultaneously.
items.answer:
### 1. Lower bound on relevance

For any decoder $r_\psi(y\mid t)$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[-\log r_\psi(Y\mid T)]
&=H(Y\mid T)
+
\mathbb E_TD_{\mathrm{KL}}
\bigl(P_{Y\mid T}\|r_\psi(\cdot\mid T)\bigr)\\
&\ge H(Y\mid T).
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}
I(T;Y)
&=H(Y)-H(Y\mid T)\\
&\ge H(Y)+\mathbb E[\log r_\psi(Y\mid T)].
\end{aligned}
$$

The bound is tight exactly when

$$
r_\psi(y\mid t)=P(y\mid t)
$$

almost surely under $P_T$.

### 2. Upper bound on rate

Let

$$
q(t)=\int q(t\mid x)p(x)\,dx.
$$

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_XD_{\mathrm{KL}}(q(T\mid X)\|r(T))
&=\mathbb E_{X,T}\log\frac{q(t\mid x)}{r(t)}\\
&=\mathbb E_{X,T}\log\frac{q(t\mid x)}{q(t)}
+
\mathbb E_T\log\frac{q(t)}{r(t)}\\
&=I_q(X;T)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q(T)\|r(T)).
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus KL to the chosen prior upper-bounds $I(X;T)$.

### 3. Simultaneous tightness

Both bounds are tight when

$$
r_\psi(y\mid t)=P(y\mid t)
$$

and

$$
r(t)=q(t).
$$

The first requires an exact variational decoder; the second requires the prior to equal the aggregate posterior. A restricted parametric model may not satisfy either condition.

---

items.title: Exercise 4. VAE: the likelihood defines distortion
items.prompt:
Consider

$$
p_\theta(x\mid z)
=
\mathcal N(\mu_\theta(z),\sigma^2I).
$$


1. Derive the negative log-likelihood and its connection to MSE.

2. Explain why changing $\sigma^2$ changes the relative weighting of distortion and rate even when $\beta=1$.

3. Derive
   $$
   \mathcal R
   =
   I(X;Z)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q(Z)\|p(Z)).
   $$
items.answer:
For a $d$-dimensional observation,

$$
p_\theta(x\mid z)
=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-d/2}
\exp\left[-\frac{\|x-\mu_\theta(z)\|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right].
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{
-\log p_\theta(x\mid z)
=
\frac d2\log(2\pi\sigma^2)
+
\frac{\|x-\mu_\theta(z)\|^2}{2\sigma^2}
}.
$$

At fixed $\sigma^2$, minimizing NLL is equivalent to minimizing MSE. The coefficient of MSE is $1/(2\sigma^2)$, however, so changing $\sigma^2$ changes the relative strength of reconstruction and KL-rate even at formal $\beta=1$.

For the rate decomposition, add and subtract $\log q(z)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal R
&=\mathbb E_{X,Z}\log\frac{q(z\mid x)}{p(z)}\\
&=\mathbb E_{X,Z}\log\frac{q(z\mid x)}{q(z)}
+
\mathbb E_Z\log\frac{q(z)}{p(z)}\\
&=I_q(X;Z)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q(Z)\|p(Z)).
\end{aligned}
$$

---

items.title: Exercise 5. Quantization: which rate–distortion problem is being posed?
items.answer:
A careful answer may use the following choices.

### Source alphabet

One must decide whether the source consists of individual weights, weight blocks, matrix rows or columns, or channel groups together with activation statistics. Classical theory also requires a probabilistic ensemble, not merely one fixed matrix without a source model.

### Actual rate

It may include quantized values or indices, scales and zero-points, codebooks, group boundaries, sparsity metadata, padding and alignment, and container headers. Nominal bit-width is therefore not always the actual number of bits per parameter.

### Possible distortions

Examples are:


1. $\|W-\widehat W\|_2^2$;

2. $\mathbb E\|WX-\widehat W X\|_2^2$ on calibration activations;

3. an increase in NLL or KL between the original and quantized predictive distributions;

4. a change in a downstream metric.

### Why the Gaussian bound does not bound accuracy

$D\ge\sigma^2 2^{-2R}$ assumes an i.i.d. Gaussian source, squared error, and an optimal long-block code. Downstream accuracy is a nonlinear function of the entire network, data distribution, and decision boundaries. Equal weight MSE can have very different functional effects in different parameter directions.

---

items.title: Exercise 6. Python: discrete IB and the VAE-rate decomposition
items.answer:
The script performs three independent checks.

### Rate–distortion curves

The Bernoulli curve decreases from $h_2(p)$ at $D=0$ to zero at $D=p$. The Gaussian curve diverges as $D\downarrow0$ and becomes zero for $D\ge\sigma^2$.

### Toy Information Bottleneck

At small $\beta$, the penalty on $I(X;T)$ dominates. The optimal representation is nearly unused:

$$
I(X;T)\approx0,
\qquad
I(T;Y)\approx0.
$$

As $\beta$ grows, the representation separates inputs with different $P(Y\mid x)$. Relevance saturates near $I(X;Y)$ because $X$ contains no more information about $Y$. Meanwhile $I(X;T)$ can continue to grow if the code preserves input details that add no predictive relevance.

### VAE-rate decomposition

Numerically one should find

$$
\mathbb E_XD_{\mathrm{KL}}(q(Z\mid X)\|p(Z))
=
I(X;Z)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q(Z)\|p(Z))
$$

to floating-point accuracy.

Replacing a good prior with a poor one leaves $I(X;Z)$ unchanged because the encoder and joint distribution are unchanged. It increases $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q(Z)\|p(Z))$ and hence the KL-rate. This is an extra mismatch cost, not extra information about the data.

---

codeFiles.source:
from __future__ import annotations

"""Reproducible numerical experiments for Module 9.

The script:
1. plots Bernoulli and Gaussian rate-distortion curves;
2. solves a finite Information Bottleneck problem by self-consistent updates;
3. verifies the exact VAE-rate decomposition on a discrete toy encoder.

All logarithms used for information quantities are base 2 unless stated otherwise.
"""

from pathlib import Path
import math

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
OUT = ROOT / "generated_experiment"
OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
EPS = 1e-15


def normalize(a: np.ndarray, axis: int = -1) -> np.ndarray:
    total = a.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)
    if np.any(total <= 0):
        raise ValueError("Cannot normalize non-positive mass")
    return a / total


def xlog2x(x: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    return np.where(x > 0, x * np.log2(x), 0.0)


def binary_entropy(p: np.ndarray | float) -> np.ndarray:
    p = np.asarray(p, dtype=float)
    p = np.clip(p, EPS, 1 - EPS)
    return -(p * np.log2(p) + (1 - p) * np.log2(1 - p))


def mutual_information(joint: np.ndarray) -> float:
    joint = np.asarray(joint, dtype=float)
    joint = joint / joint.sum()
    px = joint.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    py = joint.sum(axis=0, keepdims=True)
    ratio = np.divide(joint, px @ py, out=np.ones_like(joint), where=joint > 0)
    return float(np.sum(np.where(joint > 0, joint * np.log2(ratio), 0.0)))


def kl_rows(p: np.ndarray, q: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Return all pairwise KL divergences D(p_i || q_j) in bits."""
    p = np.asarray(p, dtype=float)
    q = np.asarray(q, dtype=float)
    p_safe = np.clip(p, EPS, 1)
    q_safe = np.clip(q, EPS, 1)
    return np.sum(p[:, None, :] * (np.log2(p_safe[:, None, :]) - np.log2(q_safe[None, :, :])), axis=-1)


def plot_rate_distortion() -> None:
    p = 0.25
    d_b = np.linspace(0, p, 250)
    r_b = binary_entropy(p) - binary_entropy(d_b)
    r_b[-1] = 0.0

    sigma2 = 1.0
    d_g = np.geomspace(0.01, sigma2, 250)
    r_g = 0.5 * np.log2(sigma2 / d_g)

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.6, 5.0))
    ax.plot(d_b, r_b, label=r"Bernoulli($p=0.25$), Hamming")
    ax.plot(d_g, r_g, label=r"Gaussian($\sigma^2=1$), MSE")
    ax.set_xlabel("Allowed distortion D")
    ax.set_ylabel("Rate R(D), bits/source symbol")
    ax.set_title("Two rate-distortion benchmarks")
    ax.legend()
    ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(OUT / "M9_experiment_rate_distortion.png", dpi=180)
    plt.close(fig)


def ib_metrics(px: np.ndarray, py_given_x: np.ndarray, qt_given_x: np.ndarray) -> tuple[float, float]:
    pxt = px[:, None] * qt_given_x
    ixt = mutual_information(pxt)
    pty = np.einsum("x,xt,xy->ty", px, qt_given_x, py_given_x)
    ity = mutual_information(pty)
    return ixt, ity


def solve_ib(
    px: np.ndarray,
    py_given_x: np.ndarray,
    n_t: int,
    beta: float,
    rng: np.random.Generator,
    restarts: int = 24,
    max_iter: int = 5000,
    tol: float = 1e-12,
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, float, float, float]:
    """Solve a finite IB problem by self-consistent updates.

    Returns q(t|x), I(X;T), I(T;Y), and the IB objective I(X;T)-beta I(T;Y).
    Multiple random restarts are used because the fixed-point equations may have
    several stationary solutions.
    """
    best: tuple[np.ndarray, float, float, float] | None = None
    n_x = px.size

    for restart in range(restarts):
        if restart == 0:
            qtx = np.full((n_x, n_t), 1.0 / n_t)
            qtx += 1e-3 * rng.random((n_x, n_t))
        else:
            qtx = rng.dirichlet(np.ones(n_t), size=n_x)
        qtx = normalize(qtx, axis=1)

        for _ in range(max_iter):
            pt = px @ qtx
            pt = np.clip(pt, EPS, None)
            pyt = np.einsum("x,xt,xy->ty", px, qtx, py_given_x)
            pyt = normalize(pyt, axis=1)
            distortion = kl_rows(py_given_x, pyt)

            # Exponents use natural exp. Convert KL bits to nats by ln(2).
            log_new = np.log(pt)[None, :] - beta * math.log(2.0) * distortion
            log_new -= log_new.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
            new = normalize(np.exp(log_new), axis=1)
            if np.max(np.abs(new - qtx)) < tol:
                qtx = new
                break
            qtx = new

        ixt, ity = ib_metrics(px, py_given_x, qtx)
        objective = ixt - beta * ity
        candidate = (qtx.copy(), ixt, ity, objective)
        if best is None or objective < best[3] - 1e-11:
            best = candidate

    assert best is not None
    return best


def run_ib_experiment() -> list[tuple[float, float, float]]:
    px = np.full(6, 1 / 6)
    # Three progressively more positive regions. Neighboring states have similar
    # predictive distributions, making the bottleneck geometry visible.
    p1 = np.array([0.03, 0.08, 0.30, 0.70, 0.92, 0.97])
    py_given_x = np.column_stack([1 - p1, p1])
    rng = np.random.default_rng(20260713)
    betas = np.array([0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.40, 0.75, 1.25, 2.0, 3.5, 6.0, 10.0, 18.0])
    rows: list[tuple[float, float, float]] = []

    for beta in betas:
        _, ixt, ity, _ = solve_ib(px, py_given_x, n_t=6, beta=float(beta), rng=rng)
        rows.append((float(beta), ixt, ity))

    ixy = mutual_information(px[:, None] * py_given_x)

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 5.4))
    ixt = np.array([r[1] for r in rows])
    ity = np.array([r[2] for r in rows])
    ax.plot(ixt, ity, marker="o", label="IB fixed points")
    for beta, x, y in rows[::2]:
        ax.annotate(f"β={beta:g}", (x, y), xytext=(5, 5), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=8)
    ax.axhline(ixy, linestyle="--", linewidth=1.2, label=f"I(X;Y)={ixy:.3f} bits")
    ax.set_xlabel("I(X;T), bits")
    ax.set_ylabel("I(T;Y), bits")
    ax.set_title("Toy Information Bottleneck frontier")
    ax.legend()
    ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(OUT / "M9_experiment_ib_frontier.png", dpi=180)
    plt.close(fig)
    return rows


def expected_conditional_kl(px: np.ndarray, qz_given_x: np.ndarray, prior: np.ndarray) -> float:
    """Average KL in bits for normalized probability arrays, without smoothing."""
    joint = px[:, None] * qz_given_x
    positive = joint > 0
    prior_grid = np.broadcast_to(prior, qz_given_x.shape)
    # A prior must cover every latent with positive joint mass. Rows with
    # px[x] = 0 and terms with q(z|x) = 0 contribute nothing, including 0 log 0.
    if np.any(prior_grid[positive] == 0):
        return math.inf
    return float(np.sum(joint[positive] * (
        np.log2(qz_given_x[positive]) - np.log2(prior_grid[positive])
    )))


def run_rate_decomposition(bad_prior: np.ndarray | None = None) -> dict[str, float]:
    px = np.array([0.40, 0.35, 0.25])
    qz_given_x = np.array([
        [0.80, 0.15, 0.05],
        [0.20, 0.65, 0.15],
        [0.05, 0.20, 0.75],
    ])
    qz = px @ qz_given_x
    good_prior = qz.copy()
    if bad_prior is None:
        bad_prior = np.array([0.78, 0.12, 0.10])

    joint = px[:, None] * qz_given_x
    ixz = mutual_information(joint)
    # Ordinary KL is the same calculation with a single source state.
    mismatch_good = expected_conditional_kl(np.ones(1), qz[None, :], good_prior)
    mismatch_bad = expected_conditional_kl(np.ones(1), qz[None, :], bad_prior)
    rate_good = expected_conditional_kl(px, qz_given_x, good_prior)
    rate_bad = expected_conditional_kl(px, qz_given_x, bad_prior)

    if not np.isclose(rate_good, ixz + mismatch_good, atol=1e-12):
        raise AssertionError("Good-prior decomposition failed")
    if not np.isclose(rate_bad, ixz + mismatch_bad, atol=1e-12):
        raise AssertionError("Bad-prior decomposition failed")

    labels = ["I(X;Z)", "prior mismatch", "total KL-rate"]
    good = [ixz, mismatch_good, rate_good]
    bad = [ixz, mismatch_bad, rate_bad]
    x = np.arange(len(labels))
    width = 0.35
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.7, 5.0))
    ax.bar(x - width / 2, good, width, label="prior = aggregate posterior")
    finite = np.isfinite(bad)
    ax.bar(x[finite] + width / 2, np.asarray(bad)[finite], width,
           label="mismatched prior")
    for position in x[~finite] + width / 2:
        ax.text(position, 0.78, "∞", transform=ax.get_xaxis_transform(),
                ha="center", color="C1", fontsize=22)
    ax.set_xticks(x, labels)
    ax.set_ylabel("Bits")
    ax.set_title("VAE-rate decomposition: information plus prior mismatch")
    ax.legend()
    ax.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.25)
    if not np.all(finite):
        # Text annotations do not participate in Matplotlib's autoscaling.
        ax.set_xlim(-0.6, len(labels) - 0.4)
        fig.text(0.5, 0.02, "∞: prior assigns zero mass to a possible latent",
                 ha="center", fontsize=10)
    fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.06 if not np.all(finite) else 0, 1, 1))
    fig.savefig(OUT / "M9_experiment_rate_decomposition.png", dpi=180)
    plt.close(fig)

    return {
        "I(X;Z)": ixz,
        "good_mismatch": mismatch_good,
        "good_rate": rate_good,
        "bad_mismatch": mismatch_bad,
        "bad_rate": rate_bad,
    }


def main() -> None:
    plot_rate_distortion()
    rows = run_ib_experiment()
    decomposition = run_rate_decomposition()

    print("Toy IB results (bits):")
    print("beta\tI(X;T)\tI(T;Y)")
    for beta, ixt, ity in rows:
        print(f"{beta:>5g}\t{ixt:.6f}\t{ity:.6f}")

    print("\nVAE-rate decomposition (bits):")
    for key, value in decomposition.items():
        print(f"{key}: {value:.9f}")
    print("\nGenerated figures:")
    for path in sorted(OUT.glob("M9_experiment_*.png")):
        print(path.name)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

items.title: Bonus. I–MMSE for a Gaussian input
items.prompt: For $X\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$, derive the posterior mean, $\operatorname{mmse}(\gamma)$, and $I(X;Y_\gamma)$. Verify the identity and explain why the integral to infinity diverges even though differential entropy is finite.
items.answer:
Let

$$
Y_\gamma=\sqrt\gamma X+N,
\qquad
X,N\sim\mathcal N(0,1)
$$

independently. Gaussian conditioning gives

$$
\mathbb E[X\mid Y_\gamma]
=
\frac{\sqrt\gamma}{1+\gamma}Y_\gamma
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y_\gamma)=\frac1{1+\gamma}.
$$

Therefore

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{mmse}(\gamma)=\frac1{1+\gamma}
}.
$$

The Gaussian mutual information is

$$
\boxed{
I(X;Y_\gamma)=\frac12\ln(1+\gamma)
}.
$$

Indeed,

$$
\frac d{d\gamma}I(X;Y_\gamma)
=
\frac1{2(1+\gamma)}
=
\frac12\operatorname{mmse}(\gamma).
$$

But

$$
\frac12\int_0^\infty\frac{d\gamma}{1+\gamma}=\infty.
$$

This does not contradict the finiteness of

$$
h(X)=\frac12\ln(2\pi e).
$$

I–MMSE integrates the mutual information between a continuous variable and an observation of ever increasing precision, which diverges. A relation to differential entropy requires subtraction of a divergent reference term; the unrenormalized equality is false.
